barCharacter: Polly Geist. Same comic job: the one who wants the mess bigger right now, answers her own question before you can, and treats other people's stakes (death, for her; heartbreak, for Pixel) as entertainment. Only eight Polly-spoken lines exist in the corpus, so the bar twelve is filled with her route's player options and narration, marked.

I mean, I'm a ghost named Polly Geist, but you don't hear me crying.
Are you with me? Obviously you're with me. I'm hot and hot people are always right. So how do we kick this party up a notch, huh?

...If only I could think of a good lie. Help me out here. What should I say on my resume to make sure they hire me?
So tell me, how did you die? We have to share so much ghost gossip... or ghostsip as I like to call it!

The electric slide… but with actual electricity. (player option, Polly route)
I only tell how I died on the third date, boo. GHOST WINK! (player option, Polly route)
Polly Geist (22?), a party ghost with an insatiable hunger for all the wrong things. (Narrator intro)
headToHead.voice: Bar. Cover the names and Polly is identified by syntax alone: run-on clauses chained with 'Like,' 'Anyway,' 'So,' 'huh?', a question she answers herself, texting spelling, and a breezy misreading of mortal stakes. Pixel is identified by nouns (chat, stream, clip, skip, thumbnail, mod). Strip those and the shape is three to five clipped fragments ending on an imperative, which is the house default: Maximilian's 'Dreadful. Truly dreadful. Do it again.' is a Pixel line with the wig off. Only 'Do you like me or the views? The views.' uses Polly's self-answer, and it is the strongest voice line in the bank.
headToHead.construction: Tie. Pixel's best lines are tighter than Polly's and land on the last word ('Clicking anyway.', 'It was me.'). Polly's are baggier ('I need your scientific advice:') but carry an engine Pixel lacks: escalation by literalism ('fun' in 'funeral', 'what kills people'). Pixel's lower half loses on construction with tag explanations ('That's the difference.', 'That's a score.', 'That's content.').
headToHead.quotable: Bar. 'It's so hard to keep track of what kills people!' and 'put the fun back in funeral' are lines people repeat out of context. Pixel has three clippable lines ('Prince. Chat says scam. Clicking anyway.', 'That's stream. Clip your favourite moment. It was me.', 'Muted. Reflex. Unmuting. No, reflex again.'), and each is good rather than famous. None reveals a worldview the way 'what kills people' does.
headToHead.verdict: Bar. If both ran tonight Polly is the better written character, because her voice survives without her vocabulary and Pixel's does not.

biggestGap: Pixel's voice lives in the nouns, not the grammar: nearly every line is the same chain of three to five clipped fragments ('Bigger. No, bigger than that. Okay, now I'm watching.'), the shape Maximilian also uses, so covering the streamer vocabulary leaves nobody. In the next pass, put the short attention span in the sentence itself: one run-on line that starts on the suitor and swerves mid-clause onto Pixel or something shinier, or a question Pixel answers before the full stop. Rewrite at least half of the cardReact 'on' lines and the react lines that way, and cut T1 (chat quotes) and T2 (Bigger/Louder/Again) to five lines each.

notes: Monster Prom reference file was present and read in full; charm-notes skimmed. 191 lines judged. 115 flagged (60.2%): 33 are generic, stock or self-explaining outright, and the rest are templated. Several templates (score, chat, escalation) are moves the persona asks for. The fault is that each is done in one identical shape every time, not that the move exists. Also protect: 'My motherboard's here. Chat raised me, but she paid for it. Intentions, go.' and the ex line 'Tip: Pixel leaves at ninety-nine percent. I know. I was at ninety-nine percent.' (best line in the file, but spoken by the ex). Intro and question lines are the cleanest section: 'Why you over them? Don't say personality. Say something I can put in a thumbnail.' and 'I wake up tilted. Controller through the wall tilted.' have a voice of their own. The secret (quits at almost) is now in 11 lines and is stated outright in most of them ('I always leave', 'I leave before the end anyway', 'Almost is where I usually leave'). Keep three that slip sideways and cut the rest. The one sanctioned mid-sentence drop (the moth) is the only line that puts the attention span into the grammar, and it uses an apology and 'lovely' to do it.
